title: The History of Earth
subtitle: Formation to now, 4.54 billion years
sourceNote: Dates from the International Commission on Stratigraphy and current radiometric consensus; the earliest ones carry real uncertainty.

waypoints.name: The Moon forms
waypoints.body: A Mars-sized body called Theia hits the young Earth. The debris becomes the Moon. All of this is over inside the first one percent of your route.

waypoints.name: The oldest surviving minerals
waypoints.body: Zircon crystals from Western Australia, 4.4 billion years old. They suggest there was already liquid water.

waypoints.name: The oldest known rocks
waypoints.body: The Acasta gneiss in northern Canada. Everything older has been recycled by the planet.

waypoints.name: The first evidence of life
waypoints.body: Chemical traces in Greenland rocks, 3.7 billion years old. Life appears remarkably early and then changes very little for a very long time.

waypoints.name: The Great Oxidation Event
waypoints.body: Cyanobacteria fill the air with oxygen and poison most of what was living. It is the largest extinction in Earth's history.

waypoints.name: Complex cells
waypoints.body: One cell swallows another and keeps it. That accident becomes the mitochondria in every cell of your body.

waypoints.name: Snowball Earth
waypoints.body: Ice reaches the equator, possibly more than once. The planet is close to a total freeze.

waypoints.name: The first animals
waypoints.body: The Ediacaran biota: soft, strange, mostly unlike anything alive now. You are already eighty-six percent of the way through Earth's history.

waypoints.name: The Cambrian explosion
waypoints.body: Almost every animal body plan alive today appears within a few tens of millions of years. Eyes, shells, legs, jaws.

waypoints.name: Plants move onto land
waypoints.body: The continents turn green for the first time. Before this, every landscape on Earth was bare rock.

waypoints.name: The Great Dying
waypoints.body: The Permian extinction kills around ninety percent of marine species. Life takes millions of years to recover.

waypoints.name: The end of the dinosaurs
waypoints.body: A ten-kilometre asteroid hits the Yucatan. Non-avian dinosaurs are gone, and mammals inherit the planet.

waypoints.name: Homo sapiens
waypoints.body: Our entire species fits into the last seven thousandths of one percent of the route. On a ten kilometre walk, that is the final sixty centimetres.
